Trisha, you're chewing your nails over this band audition, so let your Deepika Maasi tell you something.

When I was fifteen, our school started a band. They needed a drummer. I had been drumming on every tiffin box and table in Pune for years. Everyone told me to go.

And I said, very calmly, "I'll fail." I could see it: my sticks slipping, the music teacher frowning, the older boys smirking at a girl on drums. It didn't feel like a fear. It felt like I already knew, the way you know tomorrow is Tuesday.

So I didn't go. I sat at home and polished my shoes, of all things.

Two years later, at my farewell, the music teacher said, "Why didn't you ever try for the band? We never found a decent drummer."

I never found out if I'd fail. That's the part that still pinches. The forecast was the only thing that actually stopped me.

I said no. I said I had a project. The truth is I'd already watched the whole evening in my head: long silences, me talking too much about lenses, Naveen checking his phone, both of us relieved when it ended. I knew it would be awkward, so why go and be disappointed?

Uma, 20, came back today. Last week she mentioned that a classmate, Ravi, had asked her to dinner on Saturday. Today she told me she had said no.

At the small architecture firm in Chennai, Rakesh closed his laptop with a sigh. "They'll reject it. The client wants glass towers, and we've given them a courtyard house. I'd put money on it."

Deepak, his manager, pulled up a chair. Deepak privately thought the design was brilliant and was sure of a yes. "Okay. Is that something you know, or a guess?"

Rakesh paused. "A guess. A strong guess."

"Then let's test it. Write down your prediction. I'll write mine." Deepak folded a sticky note: "Yes, full design." Rakesh wrote: "Rejected outright."

On Friday the client called. They didn't want the courtyard house for their main site. But they loved the shaded verandas and asked the firm to design a small community library for their second plot.

Deepak laughed and stuck both notes on the board. "We were both wrong."

Rakesh looked at the notes for a long moment, then started a new folder: "Library".

The warehouse office in Ludhiana smelled of cardboard and tea.

"Kiran ma'am, there's no point sending the canteen bid," Baljeet said. "The school will pick the bigger supplier. They always do."

Kiran looked up from the invoices. "Always?"

"Well. Every time I've heard of."

"How many times is that?"

He thought. "Two."

"So is it a fact or a forecast?"

"...A forecast."

"Good. Forecasts can be tested. Write yours down." She tore a page from her diary. "I'll write mine."

He wrote, "They'll say no." She wrote, "They'll say yes to all of it."

"And if you're wrong?" she asked.

"Then I'll bring the samosas."

Ten days later, the school's email arrived. They had accepted the fruit and milk supply, but not the snacks.

Baljeet read it twice. "Half yes."

Kiran grinned. "Half wrong, both of us. Samosas are on me."

Elizabeth joined us in March and has been sure she cannot lead Saturday storytime. "The children will get bored and start running around," she said. "I'm ninety percent sure."

I asked her to write that number down, then try a small version: ten minutes, one picture book, five children, with me in the room. Afterwards she wrote what actually happened: "Two wriggled. One asked for the book again. Nobody ran."

We've kept this up for six weeks. Every Saturday she writes her forecast and her confidence before, and what happened after. Her first forecasts were all ninety or above for disaster. Last week she wrote, "Some will lose focus by the end. Sixty percent." And that is roughly what happened, which she laughed about.

The record seems to be making her guesses more accurate, and much less harsh on herself.

Next step: next month she'll lead the full thirty minutes, and I'll sit at the back.

— Anjali

Thursday, Bengaluru. Entry 9 in the prediction notebook.

Vijay started this for me three weeks ago when I refused to try Kannada at the vegetable market. My forecast then: "They'll laugh, I'll freeze, I'll go home with nothing. 95% sure."

Today's plan was small: ask the tomato lady the price in Kannada. Only that.

Before: 80% sure it'll go badly.

What happened: I got one word wrong. She corrected me, smiling, and then told me her daughter is learning Hindi and mixes things up too. I bought tomatoes and coriander. She threw in two green chillies free.

Tomorrow: ask the bus conductor something.

I'm Joel. Last month I had to present the water-tank repair plan to our housing society committee, and the chair, Mrs Farzana Shaikh, is known for grilling people.

passage:
In their flat in Salt Lake, Kolkata, Santosh, eleven, had written two rules inside his cupboard door: MUST BE FIRST IN EVERY TEST. MUST NEVER CRY.

On Thursday he came third in the class quiz. On the way home his water bottle spilled over his notebook, and before he could stop it, he was crying in the auto.

At home he stared at the cupboard door. Both rules, broken in one day. He felt like the worst boy in the world.

His aunt Hansa read the door. "Who made these?"

"Me."

"Then you can change them. What rule would a kind teacher give you?"

Santosh wiped his nose. He didn't answer. But he didn't close the cupboard either.

qa.q: Where had Santosh written his two rules?
qa.a: On the inside of his cupboard door.

qa.q: Why did Santosh feel like the worst boy in the world after Thursday?
qa.a: He had broken both of his rules in one day, coming third and crying, so he felt he had failed completely. His strict rules turned two ordinary things into shame.

qa.q: What choice did Hansa offer Santosh, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: She pointed out that he made the rules and so could change them, and asked what rule a kind teacher would give. That invites him to write gentler rules instead of feeling guilty.

qa.q: If you were Hansa, reading those rules on the door, what would you want Santosh to understand?
qa.a: That coming third and crying over a wet notebook are ordinary, not shameful. Hansa would probably want him to swap the rules for kinder ones he can actually live with.

grounding: A boy who tells himself he must always be first and never cry feels ashamed when he comes third and cries, and his aunt questions the rules.

passage:
Friday

Papa booked the trip to Mussoorie for next weekend. The whole family. He didn't ask me. He SHOULD know I have the inter-school quiz finals that Sunday. I've been preparing for weeks. A good father would just know.

I didn't say anything at dinner. I just ate fast and left. Mummy asked if I was okay and I said "fine" in a voice that meant not fine. "Our son is sulking," she told Papa. She should have understood why.

Then I messaged Dolma to come over tomorrow and she said she has her cousin's engagement. Again. Best friends should be free when you need them. That's the whole point.

Now I'm lying here angry at everyone. Papa, Mummy, Dolma. Nobody even knows why.

...Which, okay, is maybe the problem. I didn't tell Papa about the date. I told Dolma nothing about why I needed her.

But they still should have known.

— Sahil

qa.q: What event does Sahil have on the Sunday of the trip?
qa.a: The inter-school quiz finals.

qa.q: Why does Sahil feel angry at everyone, even though nobody knows why?
qa.a: He believes his parents and Dolma should understand and be available without being told, so when they don't, he feels let down. The "should" rules make his resentment grow faster than any conversation.

qa.q: What turning point does Sahil almost reach, and what could he do next?
qa.a: He notices that he never told Papa the date or told Dolma why he needed her. Tomorrow he could tell Papa about the finals and tell Dolma what's going on, instead of waiting for them to guess.

qa.q: How might Papa feel if he later learns about the quiz finals?
qa.a: Papa would likely feel surprised and sorry, wishing Sahil had told him before he booked. He might also feel hurt at being expected to guess.

grounding: A teenage boy believes his parents should know his plans and his friend should always be free, and his resentment grows faster than any conversation.
